title: An annual retreat
hookLine: a few days away each year: the Buddhist rains retreat began when monks were told to stop traveling and stay put
tomorrow: the dying Buddha named four places worth a journey. which four?

cards: Some vacations need a vacation after them: three cities, two flights, an itinerary down to the hour. The Buddha's monks had a version of that problem.
They walked from town to town, teaching and begging for food, in every season, including the rains. And people started to complain. Not about the teaching.
About the walking. It was a fair complaint, and the Buddha took it seriously. The rule that answered them still shapes the Buddhist year.

teach.b: The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, keeps the complaint. These monks travel in every season, even the rains, trampling the young green shoots and the small creatures living in them.
Other wanderers stay in one place for the rains.

teach.h: EVEN BIRDS STAY IN THEIR NESTS.
teach.b: Even the birds build nests in the treetops and stay put. The Buddha heard it and made a rule: in the rainy season, monks enter vassa, the rains retreat.
They choose one place, and they stay. Theravada monks keep that retreat to this day, and lay people visit the monasteries with food and come to hear teaching.

teach.h: PAVARANA: TELL ME WHERE I WENT WRONG.
teach.b: At the end comes a day called Pavarana, when each monk invites the others to tell him where he went wrong. Then lay people bring cloth for new robes. Look at what the retreat is.
It isn't getting away to somewhere nicer. It's stopping the travel. Staying in one spot long enough for something to grow, and not trampling the green shoots while you're at it.
And it ends with honesty, not souvenirs.
An annual retreat on your own path can borrow that shape: a few days each year when you stop moving, stay in one place, and come back ready to hear what a friend has been meaning to tell you.

how: Theravada monks keep vassa, the rains retreat, staying in one monastery for the rainy season; it ends with Pavarana, when monks invite each other's correction, and lay people offer cloth for robes. People on other paths also take a few days of retreat each year.

o: a few days each year of stopping and staying in one place
a yearly work trip where teams plan the next quarter
a long holiday spent touring as many cities as you can

games.q: your work offers a "wellness retreat": a new city each day and a packed schedule. by vassa's shape, what's missing?
o: staying put: vassa stops the travel so practice can grow in one place.
more rest stops: vassa was a break for monks tired from walking.
nothing: any trip away from work counts as a retreat.
games.why: The rule began because the walking itself did harm. Vassa means choosing one place and staying, then ending with honest correction.

practice: Open your calendar for the coming year and find a few days you could stop: a long weekend at a guesthouse, a cabin, or your own home with the phone off. Write the dates down.
For the rest of the sit, stay right where you are, as if the rains had started outside.

wordCard.voice: An annual retreat: a few days a year of staying put, shaped like the monks' rains retreat, vassa.

orig.note: Pali: rain, the rainy season. Entering vassa means the monks' rains retreat.

carryVoice: Your line: away. In the rains retreat, away means staying in one place. That's day 1643.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga III.1 (people complain that monks travel in the rains, crushing green herbs and small life; even birds stay in their nests; the Buddha prescribes vassa)
Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga IV (Pavarana at the end of vassa) and VII (kathina, cloth for robes)
